speaker: Paul Clement
title: Ep. 38 | Constitutional Chats | Paul Clement
question: In U.S. constitutional law, how do Bill of Rights guarantees written to restrict Congress end up binding most—but not all—state actions?
guest: It gets complicated because the justices on the Supreme Court didn't just say, 'Wouldn't it be great if all of these Bill of Rights provisions that as written apply only to the federal government applied to the states?' They've done it through a legal doctrine called incorporation. The 14th Amendment, which was enacted right after the Civil War as part of Reconstruction, does prohibit the states from doing things. It's written differently from the Bill of Rights and says, 'No state shall deny equal protection, or shall deny due process.' Over the years, the justices have asked what due process means, and they've essentially said most of the guarantees of the Bill of Rights are part of that due process protection. So they incorporate the first eight amendments through the 14th Amendment. But it's a tricky enough move that it's easy for a justice to say, 'Maybe I'm on board with that for the Double Jeopardy Clause, but not for the Establishment Clause.' And no justice thinks the federal civil jury trial right applies to the states. So there's play in the joints in the doctrine.

points.core: The original Bill of Rights text restricted only the federal government, not states.
points.note: Accept: noting the first eight amendments as written limit Congress/federal power rather than state governments. Do not credit: claiming the original 1791 Bill of Rights bound states directly.

points.core: Courts apply most guarantees to states through the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause.
points.note: Accept: selective incorporation doctrine reading Bill of Rights protections into the post-Civil War 14th Amendment's explicit restriction on states. Do not credit: citing the Supremacy Clause or Tenth Amendment as the incorporation vehicle.

points.core: Clause-by-clause incorporation leaves doctrinal room to exclude specific provisions like civil jury trials.
points.note: Accept: selective/piecemeal incorporation ('play in the joints') explaining why non-incorporated rights such as the Seventh Amendment civil jury trial right do not bind states and why individual justices can contest incorporating clauses like the Establishment Clause. Do not credit: claiming all Bill of Rights provisions apply automatically to states.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The mechanism is the incorporation doctrine. The Bill of Rights originally restrained only the federal government, as the Supreme Court confirmed in Barron v. Baltimore (1833). After the Civil War, the Fourteenth Amendment (1868) forbade states from depriving any person of "life, liberty, or property, without due process of law." Although the Slaughter-House Cases (1873) gutted the amendment's Privileges or Immunities Clause as a vehicle, the Court later used the Due Process Clause instead.

It did so through "selective incorporation": rather than applying the Bill of Rights wholesale, the Court asked, right by right, whether a guarantee is fundamental to the American scheme of ordered liberty or deeply rooted in the nation's history and tradition. Over the twentieth century, nearly all were held to apply to the states, including speech, religion, search and seizure, counsel, and more recently the right to bear arms (McDonald v. Chicago, 2010) and the ban on excessive fines (Timbs v. Indiana, 2019).

A few remain unincorporated: the Fifth Amendment's grand jury requirement, the Seventh Amendment's civil jury right, and the Third Amendment (never addressed by the Supreme Court).

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The Bill of Rights originally bound only the federal government. The Supreme Court said so in *Barron v. Baltimore* (1833), and the First Amendment's text ("Congress shall make no law") reflects that. The change came with the Fourteenth Amendment (1868), which forbids states to deprive anyone of "life, liberty, or property, without due process of law." The *Slaughter-House Cases* (1873) gutted the amendment's Privileges or Immunities Clause, so the Court used the Due Process Clause instead. Through **selective incorporation**, it absorbed individual guarantees that are "fundamental to our scheme of ordered liberty" and "deeply rooted in this Nation's history and tradition" (*Duncan v. Louisiana*, 1968; *McDonald v. Chicago*, 2010).

Incorporation went right by right. Examples include free speech (*Gitlow*, 1925), the exclusionary rule (*Mapp*, 1961), the right to counsel (*Gideon*, 1963), gun rights (*McDonald*), excessive fines (*Timbs*, 2019) and unanimous criminal juries (*Ramos*, 2020). An incorporated right applies to states exactly as it does to the federal government.

A few guarantees remain unincorporated. These are the Fifth Amendment's grand-jury indictment requirement (*Hurtado*, 1884), the Seventh Amendment's civil jury trial right, and the Third Amendment's ban on quartering soldiers. The Court has only assumed that the ban on excessive bail applies to states. States may still provide these protections under their own constitutions.

After the Fourteenth Amendment barred states from depriving anyone of life, liberty, or property without due process of law, the Court began interpreting its Due Process Clause to protect specific Bill of Rights guarantees against state and local governments.
